subject: biology
prompt: This is a cross-section of a young stem. Tap the tissue that carries **water and minerals** up from the roots.

image.alt: Cross-section of a young stem with numbered markers

hint: Look inside each bundle for the wide, round tubes on the side nearer the centre.
explanation: **Xylem** lies on the inner side of each vascular bundle. Its **vessels** and **tracheids** are tubular, thick-walled cells that carry water and minerals upward, and they also give the plant strength. **Phloem**, on the outer side of the same bundle, carries food instead.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the tissue that carries **food made in the leaves** to other parts of the plant.

image.alt: Cross-section of a young stem with numbered markers

hint: In each bundle it lies on the outer side, towards the epidermis.
explanation: **Phloem** sits on the outer side of every vascular bundle. Its **sieve tubes**, joined end to end through perforated walls, carry food from the leaves to the rest of the plant. Unlike xylem, phloem is made mostly of **living** cells.

subject: biology
prompt: The stem of a dicot plant gets **thicker** year after year. Tap the ring of dividing cells that causes this.

image.alt: Cross-section of a young stem with numbered markers

hint: It is a thin, continuous ring running between the two conducting tissues.
explanation: The **lateral meristem** is a ring of actively dividing cells along the circumference of the stem, here between the xylem and the phloem. Its cells add new cells both inwards and outwards, so the stem's **girth** increases. The epidermis protects and the sclerenchyma supports; neither of them divides to thicken the stem.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the region whose dividing cells make this sapling's **stem grow taller**.

image.alt: A young sapling with numbered markers

hint: Growth in length happens at the very tip.
explanation: **Apical meristems** sit at the tips of shoots and roots. The **shoot apical meristem** at the stem tip divides continuously, so the stem grows in length. The root tip also has an apical meristem, but it lengthens the root, not the stem.

subject: biology
prompt: Mowed grass and trimmed hedges grow back because of the **intercalary meristem**. Tap where this meristem is found on the sapling.

image.alt: A young sapling with numbered markers

hint: Look for the point on the stem where leaves are attached.
explanation: The **intercalary meristem** lies at the base of an internode, just above a **node** (the point where leaves or branches arise). It helps grasses regrow after mowing or grazing and makes a cut hedge turn bushy. The meristems at the shoot and root tips are **apical** meristems.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the part of the root that greatly **increases the surface area** for absorbing water and minerals.

image.alt: A young sapling with numbered markers

hint: Look for fine, hair-like outgrowths of the root's outer cells.
explanation: **Root hairs** are hair-like projections of the root's **epidermal** cells. They greatly increase the surface in contact with the soil, so more water and minerals are absorbed. The root tip holds the root apical meristem, which lengthens the root.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the short branches of this nerve cell that **receive signals** from other neurons.

image.alt: A nerve cell with numbered markers

hint: They are the many short branches spreading out from the cell body.
explanation: **Dendrites** are short, branched extensions that receive messages from other neurons. The **cell body** contains the nucleus and controls the cell, the long **axon** carries the message away, and the **axon terminals** pass it on to other cells.

subject: biology
prompt: Sit on a chair and swing your lower leg up. The knee stops at a limit and does not slip out of place (dislocate). Tap the tissue that **joins bone to bone** and keeps the joint steady like this.

image.alt: Side view of a knee joint with numbered markers

hint: It is a band at the side of the joint, stretching from the upper bone to the lower bone.
explanation: **Ligaments** connect bone to bone. They keep a joint stable, limit how far it can move and help prevent dislocation. **Tendons** look similar but connect muscle to bone, and the blue **cartilage** cushions the ends of the bones.

subject: biology
prompt: Shake your head to say 'no'. Tap the **pivot joint** that lets your head turn from side to side.

image.alt: A cartoon human skeleton with numbered markers

hint: It is where the skull rests on top of the backbone.
explanation: The skull joins the backbone at a **pivot joint**, which lets the head turn side to side like a doorknob. The shoulder is a **ball and socket** joint, the elbow and knee are **hinge** joints, and the bones of the skull meet at **fixed** joints.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **vertebral column**. It is a stack of small bones with cartilage discs that let you bend and twist safely.

image.alt: A cartoon human skeleton with numbered markers

hint: It runs down the middle of the back from the base of the skull.
explanation: The **vertebral column** (backbone or spine) is a flexible column of small bones called **vertebrae**. A **cartilage disc** between each pair acts as a cushion, so we can bend and twist without injuring the spinal cord inside. It supports the body and helps us stand upright.

subject: biology
prompt: Plants stay fixed in one place, but a tall tree stands upright for years. Which feature of plant cells helps plant tissues the most in giving this support?

image.alt: A plant cell

options.text: Cells that can change shape easily
A rigid cell wall around each cell

hint: Animal cells lack this layer, which is why they can change shape.
explanation: Plants cannot move, so their tissues must keep them firm and upright. Plant cells have a **cell wall** that gives rigidity and strength. Animal cells lack a cell wall and can change shape easily, which suits movement from place to place.

subject: biology
prompt: Two onion bulbs grew roots in jars of water. On day 3, about 1 cm of the root tips in **Jar B** was cut off. What does the graph tell you?

image.alt: Line graph of onion root length over seven days for Jar A and Jar B

options.text: Roots grow equally along their whole length
Cutting the tips makes roots grow faster
Roots grow in length only from their tips
Jar B's roots stopped because its water ran out

hint: Compare the two lines after day 3.
explanation: After the cut, the Jar B line stays flat while Jar A keeps rising. So the growth zone is at the **tip**, where cells divide continuously: the **root apical meristem**. If roots grew along their whole length, the cut roots would have kept getting longer.

subject: biology
prompt: Use the graph. On **day 7**, how much longer are the roots in Jar A than the roots in Jar B?

image.alt: Line graph of onion root length over seven days for Jar A and Jar B

hint: Read both lines at day 7, then subtract.
explanation: At day 7, Jar A = **7 cm** and Jar B = **2 cm**, so the difference is 7 − 2 = **5 cm**. Using Jar B's day-3 length (3 cm) gives 4 cm, which forgets that 1 cm was cut off and never grew back. Adding the lengths (9 cm) or reading only Jar A (7 cm) does not give a difference.

subject: biology
prompt: A disc of wood is cut from a young tree, and its bark is removed. The disc is **24 cm across** and has **6 annual rings**. On average, by how much did the trunk's **radius** grow each year?

image.alt: A cross-section disc of a tree trunk showing rings

hint: The radius is half the diameter, and one ring stands for one year.
explanation: Radius = 24 ÷ 2 = **12 cm**, laid down over **6 years** (one ring per year), so 12 ÷ 6 = **2 cm per year**. Dividing the diameter by 6 (4 cm) forgets to halve it, 6 ÷ 24 turns the ratio upside down, and counting each light and dark band as a separate year doubles the count to 12, giving 1 cm. The rings are made by the **lateral meristem**.

subject: biology
prompt: The chart shows the trunk diameter at breast height (DBH) of a teak tree at different ages. Its number of annual rings was always equal to its age. What was the **average increase in DBH per year** between the ages of **10 and 20 years**?

image.alt: Bar chart of a teak tree's trunk diameter at different ages

hint: Find the change in DBH, then divide by the change in age.
explanation: DBH rose from **8 cm** at 10 years to **24 cm** at 20 years: (24 − 8) ÷ (20 − 10) = 16 ÷ 10 = **1.6 cm per year**. Dividing 24 by 20 (1.2) uses the whole lifetime instead of that decade, 16 cm forgets to divide by the 10 years, and 0.8 cm is the rate for the first 10 years only. This growth in girth comes from the **lateral meristem**.

subject: biology
prompt: Riya's mother weighs **50 kg**. An adult's bones make up about **12–15%** of body weight. Estimate the mass of her bones.

image.alt: A bathroom weighing scale reading 50 kg

hint: Multiply the body weight by 12/100 and by 15/100.
explanation: 12% of 50 kg = 0.12 × 50 = **6 kg** and 15% of 50 kg = 0.15 × 50 = **7.5 kg**, so her bones weigh about **6–7.5 kg**. Writing the percentages straight as kilograms gives 12–15 kg, misplacing the decimal point (0.012 × 50 and 0.015 × 50) gives 0.6–0.75 kg, and subtracting the percentages from 50 gives 35–38 kg.

subject: biology
prompt: A donor gives **350 mL** of blood. Plasma makes up about **55%** of blood volume. Roughly how much of the donated blood is plasma?

image.alt: A blood sample that has settled into two layers in a test tube

hint: Plasma is the larger, straw-coloured layer. Find 55% of 350.
explanation: Plasma ≈ 55% of 350 mL = 0.55 × 350 = **192.5 mL**. 157.5 mL is the 45% made of **formed elements** (RBCs, WBCs and platelets); 636 mL comes from dividing by 0.55 instead of multiplying, which is more than was donated; and 55 mL treats the percentage as a volume.

subject: biology
prompt: Which sample shows the muscle that keeps your **heart** beating throughout life?

image.alt: Muscle tissue sample P
Muscle tissue sample Q
Muscle tissue sample R

hint: Look for fibres that branch and join one another.
explanation: **Cardiac muscle** (Q) has cylindrical, **branched** fibres with one nucleus per cell and faint striations; it works rhythmically without tiring. P, with long, unbranched, striped fibres and many nuclei, is **skeletal muscle**. R, with spindle-shaped cells, one nucleus each and no stripes, is **smooth muscle**.

subject: biology
prompt: Coconut-husk fibres are hard and tough enough to make doormats. Which sample shows the cells that give them this strength?

image.alt: Plant tissue sample P
Plant tissue sample Q
Plant tissue sample R

hint: Look for cells whose walls are so thick that only a tiny space is left inside.
explanation: **Sclerenchyma** (P) has very thick walls hardened with **lignin**, and most of its cells are dead; it makes coconut husk, walnut shells and seed coats hard. Living, thin-walled **parenchyma** (Q) is soft and stores food, while **collenchyma** (R), thickened only at the corners, is flexible rather than hard.

subject: biology
prompt: Aamrapali sees a young mango sapling bend in the monsoon wind without breaking. Which sample shows the tissue that gives the young stem this **flexible support**?

image.alt: Plant tissue sample P
Plant tissue sample Q
Plant tissue sample R

hint: Look for living cells with extra thickening only at their corners.
explanation: **Collenchyma** (R) is made of living cells whose walls are thickened unevenly at the **corners** by **pectin**, which makes them flexible like rubber. It lets young stems, tendrils and leaf stalks (like coriander's) bend without breaking. If it were replaced by stiff, lignified **sclerenchyma** (Q), the stem would be more likely to snap in strong wind.

subject: biology
prompt: How does a water plant like this one manage to **float**?

image.alt: A water plant floating on a pond

options.text: Its roots are covered by a thick cuticle
Its stems are made of lignified sclerenchyma
Special parenchyma in it has large air spaces

hint: Think about what makes a life jacket float.
explanation: In aquatic plants, specialised **parenchyma** forms large **air spaces** that make the plant light, so it floats. Lignified sclerenchyma would make it hard and heavy, and a cuticle or extra root hairs do not provide buoyancy.

subject: biology
prompt: An elephant peeled a band of bark off this tree to eat it. Months later, the roots begin to starve, even though the leaves are still green and making food. Damage to which tissue best explains this? (This tissue lies just under the bark.)

image.alt: An elephant beside a tree whose bark has been stripped in a band

hint: Which tissue carries food downwards from the leaves?
explanation: **Phloem** lies just inside the bark, so a stripped band tears it away. Phloem carries food from the leaves **down** to the roots; with the band broken, food cannot pass and the roots slowly starve. **Xylem** lies deeper in the wood and carries water upward, which is why the leaves stay green for a while.

subject: biology
prompt: Sohan planted two kinds of sugarcane cuttings, A and B. After a few weeks only the **B** cuttings sprouted into new plants. What made the difference?

image.alt: Two sugarcane cuttings, A and B, planted in soil

options.text: Cutting B was planted deeper in the soil
Cutting B had a node, with meristematic tissue that can form new shoots and roots
Cutting B got more sunlight under the soil

hint: Look carefully at what cutting B has in its middle.
explanation: Only cutting B included a **node**, which carries a bud and **meristematic tissue** whose cells can still divide, so new shoots and roots grew from it. Cutting A was only internode, made of **permanent tissue** that cannot form a new plant. For a fair test, both cuttings should have the same length, soil, water and temperature.

subject: biology
prompt: This plant has **crown gall disease**. It has tumour-like swellings caused by fast, uncontrolled cell division. Which organism causes it?

image.alt: A plant stem with a large lumpy swelling near the soil

hint: The text says this germ can pass its own genetic material into plant cells.
explanation: Crown gall is caused by the bacterium *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*, which transfers some of its genetic material into plant cells. Scientists studied how it does this, and now use Agrobacterium as a tool to put useful genes into plants for better, disease-resistant crops. Helianthus annuus is the sunflower, not a germ.

subject: biology
prompt: Indian scientists **Sipra Guha Mukherjee** and **S. C. Maheshwari** made an important discovery in plant tissue culture. What did they achieve?

image.alt: Cells growing into a small plantlet in culture dishes

options.text: Grew complete plants from anthers on an artificial nutrient medium
Discovered the bacterium that causes crown gall
First grew a carrot plant from a single phloem cell
Wrote the Kannada book Hasuru Honnu

hint: Anthers are the parts of a flower that make pollen.
explanation: Guha Mukherjee and Maheshwari developed **complete plants through anther culture**, on an artificial nutrient medium under controlled laboratory conditions; this helped crop improvement. Growing carrot plants from single phloem cells was **F. C. Steward's** work, and Hasuru Honnu was written by botanist **B. G. L. Swamy**.

subject: biology
prompt: In 1958, **F. C. Steward** took single cells from a carrot's phloem. He grew them in a nutrient medium and got whole new carrot plants. What does this show?

image.alt: A carrot, a slice cut from it, and a flask of liquid with cells swirling

options.text: Only meristematic cells can ever divide
Phloem cells turn into xylem when kept in sugar
Animal cells can regenerate whole animals in the same way
Some mature plant cells can dedifferentiate, divide and redifferentiate into a whole plant

hint: The cells were already specialised, yet they formed every part of a new plant.
explanation: Steward's phloem cells first **dedifferentiated** (regained the ability to divide) into a mass of unspecialised cells, which then **redifferentiated** into roots, shoot and a complete plant. This ability is **totipotency**, like a zygote developing into a whole organism. It disproves the idea that only meristematic cells can divide, and it tells us nothing about animal cells.

subject: biology
prompt: As a stem grows older, some cells under its epidermis start dividing again. They form the **cork cambium**, which makes the bark. Which statement about the **cork cells** it produces is correct?

image.alt: Close-up of the outer layers of an old tree stem

options.text: They are dead, tightly packed and impermeable to water and gases
They are living cells with large air spaces between them
They carry food from the leaves to the roots
They form a type of apical meristem

hint: Bark has to keep water in and germs out.
explanation: The **cork cambium** acts as a lateral meristem near the surface of older stems. The **cork cells** it makes are **dead**, compactly arranged and contain a substance that makes them **impermeable to water and gases**, forming protective bark. Living cells with air spaces describe parenchyma, and carrying food is the job of phloem.

subject: biology
prompt: The image shows pores on a leaf surface opening and closing. What would most likely happen if a plant's leaves and stems had **none of these pores**?

image.alt: Close-up of a leaf surface with pores opening and closing

options.text: The plant would lose water much faster
Gas exchange and transpiration would almost stop, weakening the pull that draws water up the xylem
The roots would absorb more minerals

hint: These pores let gases in and water vapour out.
explanation: **Stomata** are pores in the epidermis used for **gaseous exchange** and **transpiration**, the loss of water vapour. Transpiration creates a **transpiration pull** that helps draw water up the xylem and also helps remove wastes. Without stomata, gas exchange and this pull would nearly stop, so the plant would lose less water, not more.

subject: biology
prompt: Your **12 pairs of ribs** form a strong cage. But your chest still rises and falls as you breathe. What allows the rib cage to move?

image.alt: A rib cage around the lungs, moving as a person breathes

options.text: The ribs are fused to each other by fixed joints
The ribs float freely with no attachments
The ribs are attached to the spine at the back and the breastbone in front, joined by flexible cartilage
The ribs are made of muscle, not bone

hint: Look at the pale blue bands linking the ribs to the bone in the middle of the chest.
explanation: The 12 pairs of ribs are attached to the **vertebral column** at the back and the **breastbone (sternum)** in front, and are joined by flexible **cartilage**. This lets the cage expand and contract, increasing and decreasing the space in the chest so that air moves in and out of the lungs. The rib cage also protects the heart and lungs.

subject: biology
prompt: A folk dancer swings her arm in a **complete circle** at the shoulder. Which type of joint makes this possible?

image.alt: A dancer moving one arm

hint: The rounded top of the upper arm bone sits in a shallow hollow.
explanation: At the shoulder, the rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone: a **ball and socket joint**. It allows forward, backward, sideways and circular movements. A **hinge** joint (elbow, knee) bends one way only, a **pivot** joint (neck) turns side to side, and **fixed** joints (skull) do not move.

It improves **flexibility, posture and breathing**, reduces stress and helps prevent lifestyle diseases, keeping bones strong and joints flexible. **21 June** is International Yoga Day; 5 June is World Environment Day.

subject: biology
prompt: Plant tissues are organised into three **tissue systems**. To which system do parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma belong?

image.alt: Cross-section of a young plant stem

hint: This system forms the main body of the plant between the skin and the pipes.
explanation: The **ground tissue system** forms the main body of the plant between the dermal and conducting tissues, and includes **parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma**. The **dermal** system forms the protective outer covering, and the **vascular** system is made of **xylem and phloem**. There is no 'meristematic tissue system'.

subject: biology
prompt: Cells at a root tip divide again and again. Which features of these **meristematic cells** help them do this? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Two groups of plant cells, one group with a cell dividing

options.text: Tightly packed, with little or no space between cells

hint: Dividing cells are small and busy; features for storage or stiffness are missing.
explanation: **Meristematic cells** are small, with **thin walls**, a **large prominent nucleus** and **dense cytoplasm** with many organelles, and they are **tightly packed** with little or no intercellular space. **Vacuoles** are generally absent, leaving the cell full of active cytoplasm. Thick lignified walls belong to sclerenchyma, whose cells cannot divide.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these are parts of **phloem**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Different cells that make up the two conducting tissues of a plant

hint: Two of these are water-carrying tubes.
explanation: Phloem is a **complex permanent tissue** made of **sieve tubes**, **companion cells**, **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres**. Sieve tubes carry food, companion cells monitor the loading and unloading of sugars, phloem parenchyma stores food, resins, tannins and latex, and the fibres give strength. **Tracheids** and **vessels** belong to xylem.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these are **connective tissues**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Red blood cells flowing through a blood vessel

hint: Blood and bone look very different but belong to the same group.
explanation: **Connective tissues** connect and support other tissues. **Blood** (watery matrix), **bone** (hard matrix with calcium and phosphorus), **cartilage** (soft, jelly-like matrix), **tendons** and ligaments are all connective tissues; they differ mainly in their **matrix**. Neurons form nervous tissue, and the intestinal lining is epithelial tissue.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these plant cells are **dead** while doing their job? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Close-up of the outer layers of an old tree stem

hint: In xylem, only the parenchyma is alive.
explanation: **Cork cells** of bark are dead and compactly arranged. In xylem, **tracheids** and **vessels** (and xylem fibres) are thick-walled, mainly sclerenchymatous cells, and **xylem parenchyma** is the only living part. **Companion cells** of phloem and **collenchyma** cells are living.

subject: biology
prompt: Each numbered tissue is a type of **epithelium**. Match it with where it is found in the body.

image.alt: Five kinds of lining tissue with numbered markers

right.text: Lining of blood vessels and lungs
Salivary and sweat glands
Skin, mouth and oesophagus
Taste buds, nostrils and inner ear
Lining of the small intestine

hint: Many layers protect; a single thin, flat layer lets gases pass through quickly.
explanation: 1 has **many layers** with flat cells on top, for **protection** in the skin, mouth and oesophagus. 2 has **tall, pillar-like cells** with a hair-like border for **absorption** in the small intestine. 3 is a **single layer of thin, flat cells** for fast diffusion in blood vessels and lungs. 4 releases **secretions**, as in salivary and sweat glands, and 5 has **receptor cells with cilia** for taste, smell, hearing and balance.

prompt: Match each muscle sample with where it is found and how its cells look.

Muscle tissue sample Q
Muscle tissue sample R

right.text: Attached to bones; long, unbranched fibres with many nuclei and stripes

prompt: Blood is a fluid connective tissue. Match each component with its role.

image.alt: Different kinds of cells flowing in a blood vessel

Watery matrix making up about 55% of blood volume

prompt: Arrange the steps of **F. C. Steward's** carrot experiment in the correct order.

image.alt: A carrot, a slice cut from it, and a flask of liquid with cells swirling

items.text: A tiny embryo-like plant develops from one cell
Cut a cross-section of the carrot root
Grow the plantlet on agar, then plant it in soil
Single cells floating in the medium begin to divide
Culture small fragments in a liquid nutrient medium; stirring frees single cells

hint: Single cells must be freed into the liquid before they can divide.
explanation: Steward cut slices of carrot root and cultured tiny **fragments** in a nutrient medium; stirring sheared **single cells** off into the liquid. These cells **divided**, one cell developed into an **embryonic plant**, and the plantlet was grown on **agar** and then in soil into an adult carrot. The mature phloem cells had dedifferentiated and then redifferentiated: **totipotency**.

prompt: Follow a drop of water from the soil to the air. Arrange its journey through the plant in order.

image.alt: Water moving up through a young plant from soil to leaves

items.text: It rises through the xylem of the stem
It escapes as water vapour through stomata
Root hairs absorb it from the soil
It reaches the cells of a leaf
It enters the xylem of the root

hint: Water enters at the bottom of the plant and leaves at the top.
explanation: **Root hairs** absorb water, which passes into the **xylem** of the root and rises through the vessels and tracheids of the stem to the leaves. It then evaporates and escapes through **stomata** (transpiration). This loss creates a **transpiration pull** that keeps the water moving up through the dead xylem cells.

items.text: Axon
Dendrites
Axon terminals
Cell body

subject: biology
prompt: How does a meristem build the permanent tissues of a plant? Arrange the steps in order.

image.alt: Two groups of plant cells, one group with a cell dividing

items.text: These cells change their shape, walls and contents
Meristematic cells divide repeatedly
They become permanent tissue with one job, such as support or transport
Some of the new cells lose the ability to divide

hint: A cell must stop dividing before it can specialise.
explanation: Meristems keep adding new cells. Some daughter cells stay meristematic, while others **lose the ability to divide**, change in structure and function and become specialised. This process is **differentiation**, and it turns meristematic tissue into **permanent tissue** for support, transport or storage.

subject: biology
prompt: You lift a cup by bending your elbow. Arrange the events in the correct order.

items.text: The tendon passes the pull on to the forearm bone
The forearm moves at the elbow joint
The brain sends a message along a nerve

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Five kinds of lining tissue side by side

assertion: The epithelium lining the lungs is well suited for the exchange of gases.

hint: For fast diffusion, would you want a thick barrier or a thin one?
explanation: A is true: the lining of the lungs and blood vessels is a **single layer of thin, flat cells**, so gases diffuse across quickly. R is false: many layers of tall cells would slow diffusion. Multi-layered epithelium is found where **protection** is needed, such as the skin.
